title: The Need to Share, Even in the Midst of Weariness
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. opens with a talk he gave on the classroom as cosmos and the Annie Dillard line that keeping what you have learned to yourself is destructive because unshared knowledge turns to ashes. He applies it to his own October exhaustion, admitting that he is so tired, and that 2026 has felt like one very long October, that sharing on his blog is the last thing he wants to do. His argument is that the way through the teacher's Wall is connection and giving what one has, even if that takes only the energy for one minute at a time. He tells tired teachers they are not alone and that what they know will turn to dust if it is not shared. The practical call is to teach from who you really are and look students in the eye as that person, and he closes with a note about his first Student Motivation Summit in San Diego.
points: Annie Dillard's claim is that withholding what you have learned harms both the people who could have benefited and the person who withheld it.
Teacher fatigue in October can be severe enough to feel funny, and it can silence the very sharing that would help.
The author's counter to exhaustion is connection and giving what one has, even if only for the single minute one is in.
Teachers hold knowledge and experience worth sharing, and it will turn to dust if it is not shared.
The immediate practice is to teach from who you are and look students in the eye as that person, which does more than it seems.
quotes: The impulse to keep to yourself what you have learned is not only shameful, it is destructive. Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you. You open the safe and find ashes.
To her, to not share what one has learned isn't merely selfish or embarrassing. It is worse than that: it inflicts loss not just on those who could benefit from the sharing, but also on the sharer.
If we choose not to share what we've learned, we'll eventually find that there's nothing left to share. The goodness, if kept locked away, reduces down to dust.

The fatigue is so extreme at times that it borders on hilarious. If you and I were truckers, working at these level of exhaustion would be criminally negligent; but since we're teachers, it's just another day in the fall.
But the way through the Wall isn't isolation; it's connection, it's giving what one has, it's sharing, and it's seeing.

So today in your class, just share it. Share who you are; teach from that person; look into your students' eyes as that person that you are. And I promise that it'll do a lot more than it will seem like it's doing.
